subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 22-year-old man performs maximal exertion on a cycle ergometer. As contraction continues, ATP is consumed more rapidly than it is regenerated, and skeletal muscle must increase glycolytic flux to sustain ATP supply. Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) catalyzes the rate-limiting step of glycolysis and is a classic allosteric enzyme.
question: Which of the following best describes the allosteric regulation of PFK-1 in this man's exercising muscle?

options.text: PFK-1 is inhibited by AMP and activated by ATP
PFK-1 is activated by citrate and inhibited by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
PFK-1 activity is unchanged because it is regulated only by covalent phosphorylation
PFK-1 is inhibited by fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and activated by ATP
PFK-1 is activated by AMP and inhibited by ATP, increasing glycolytic flux

explanation_correct: PFK-1 is allosterically activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by ATP and citrate. During intense exercise ATP falls and AMP rises, so the ATP/AMP ratio favors activation of PFK-1 and increases glycolytic flux to regenerate ATP. This allosteric control allows the muscle to match glycolytic rate to energy demand without new enzyme synthesis.

explanation_incorrect.A: The regulation is inverted: AMP, a signal of low energy charge, activates PFK-1, and ATP inhibits it when energy is abundant.
explanation_incorrect.B: Citrate inhibits PFK-1, and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the most potent activator of PFK-1 in the fed state.
explanation_incorrect.C: PFK-1 is regulated both allosterically by small metabolites and by covalent modification, so activity is not unchanged during exercise.
explanation_incorrect.D: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate activates rather than inhibits PFK-1, and ATP acts as an inhibitor rather than an activator.

educationalObjective: PFK-1 is allosterically activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by ATP and citrate, matching glycolytic flux to cellular energy demand.
